definition: Encapsulate means to express the essential features of something in a brief, compact form.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word encapsulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know encapsulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The curator asked each artist to encapsulate a whole decade in a single shop-window display.
Trim merely snips the loose edges — the piece stays essentially as long as it was; it stops far short of encapsulate.
Condense shrinks the bulk further, but it stops short of encapsulate, which closes the entire subject, undamaged, into a few words.

Distill means to boil a subject down until only its essence remains — it names the refining process itself. Encapsulate names the sealed result: the essence closed, whole and intact, into a phrase or image. You distill for hours; the line you finally keep is encapsulated.

Summarize means to shorten something to its main points, and a summary may cheerfully leave things out. Encapsulate makes a stronger promise: the whole subject, nothing essential missing, held in a few words. Every encapsulation summarizes; plenty of summaries capture only part of the story.

Encapsulate means to express the essential features of something in a brief, compact form.
The field guide encapsulates each bird in a three-line entry — silhouette, song, and the one field mark that settles arguments — so a soaked hiker can name a warbler before the page wilts.
Encapsulate is compression with nothing essential left out — the picture comes from capsule, a small sealed container.
To shorten a thing is easy; to encapsulate it is to seal the whole matter, intact, into a few words, an image, or a scene.
Encapsulate is the word when brevity keeps everything that matters: a motto, a single image, a one-line answer that holds the whole story.
Plain summarize shortens without that promise.
Its unit-mate enumerate does the opposite work — laying items out one by one at full length rather than sealing them into a phrase.

Every crewed mission gets a patch, and the design is harder than the flight suit it decorates.
For the return-to-the-Moon flight, the crew rejected forty drafts.
The problem was never beauty; it was that a patch must encapsulate the entire mission -- destination, crew, purpose, risk -- inside a circle three inches wide.
The winning design used one image: a footprint half-filled with stars, ringed by four small diamonds for the four astronauts.
Nothing was missing, the commander said, and nothing was spare; the whole voyage was in it, closed and complete, for anyone who knew how to look.
